name: Wuli-Wuli
confidence_why: The only description of Wuli-Wuli itself, Holmer 1983, states that stress is not significant and offers only a survey-wide tendency toward second-syllable prominence in longer words and phrases, while Kite and Wurm 2004, for the mutually intelligible dialect Duungidjawu, and Watson 1944, for neighbouring Kabi and Wakka, both place stress on the first syllable, so the catalog's fixed second-syllable rule is a guess from a hedged remark.
catalog_citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1983. Linguistic survey of south-eastern Queensland. Pacific Linguistics D-54. Canberra: Australian National University (online ed. CC BY-SA, hdl 1885/219890; DOI 10.15144/PL-D54). Part I 'The languages of the Wakka group': sec. 2.9 (general phonetic notes, p. 5) and Wuli-Wuli ch., sec. 10.3 'Phonology' (p. 39).
catalog_locator: Part I sec. 2.9, p. 5; Wuli-Wuli sec. 10.3, p. 39; Note 14, p. 161
catalog_quote: 2.9 Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length, as in the common Wakka-Wakka greeting wanḑá ŋin janánde where (i.e. how) are you going? Here we have two stress units, of which the former consists of two words or morphological elements; similarly in Goreng-Goreng: gilámanmin turned round, Goeng-Goeng wajálara (mountain name), goréŋ goréŋ (language name), etc. This tendency also explains the origin of certain shortened forms, e.g. (Wakka-Wakka) ga not (< waga), ḑu I (< ŋaḑu), (Barunggam) ɲaŋgu why? (< *miɲaŋgu), ɲuŋga where? (< waɲuŋga), etc. Compare the common stress pattern in Aboriginal place names of the type 'Cutháraba', 'Didíllibah', 'Barálaba', all over Queensland.14 [printed p. 5] ... 10.3 The phonetic system of Wuli-Wuli is the same as that of Wakka-Wakka and Barunggam and most of the current sound changes and general trends in the phonetic evolution are found to be the same. [printed p. 39]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Holmer, stress is non-distinctive in Wuli-Wuli as in every language of the survey; phonetically there is a general tendency for prominence on the second syllable of a word or of a longer stretch (a 'stress unit' that can span two short words), which he links to loss of initial syllables in short function words. The Wuli-Wuli chapter itself adds nothing, only that its sound system equals Wakka-Wakka/Barunggam. NB the modern grammar of the co-dialect Duungidjawu (Kite & Wurm 2004:22) instead gives word-initial primary stress with alternating secondary stress and stress on all long vowels, so the dialect group's descriptions disagree.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Holmer says nothing about secondary stress for the Wakka group. (Kite & Wurm 2004:22, Duungidjawu: secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables; first syllable secondary when a long vowel in the second syllable takes primary.)
new_statements.exceptions: Holmer Note 14 (p. 161): Wakka-Wakka speakers insisted bala· 'jewfish' differed from bala 'semen' by stress and vowel quantity; Holmer found no support for the distinction. No Wuli-Wuli-specific exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Holmer's tendency is stated over 'words or utterances of some length' and 'stress units' that may comprise two words (sec. 2.10: no marked word separation in running speech), i.e. partly phrase-level rhythm rather than strictly word-level; his examples are isolated words and place names (Wakka-Wakka, Goreng-Goreng, Goeng-Goeng), none Wuli-Wuli. The statement is survey-wide, applied to Wuli-Wuli via sec. 10.3, based on three Wuli-Wuli informants (Pope family, Eidsvold/Moura, recorded 1970s).
new_statements.identity_note: Holmer's 'Wuli-Wuli' (three informants of the Pope family at Eidsvold and Moura; country around Hawkwood station / Dawson river) is the Glottolog language wuli1242 (AIATSIS E89). His stress sentence (sec. 2.9) is survey-wide, not Wuli-Wuli-specific; it reaches Wuli-Wuli through sec. 10.3 ('phonetic system.. the same as that of Wakka-Wakka and Barunggam'). Holmer treats Wuli-Wuli as 'hardly more than a dialectal variant' of Wakka-Wakka (waka1274); Kite & Wurm 2004 (and Dixon 2002) treat Wuli-Wuli, Duungidjawu (duun1241), Djagunda, Dala, Waga-Waga and Barunggam as dialects of one 'Waga-Waga language', and their initial-stress rule (p. 22) describes Duungidjawu only.

readall_conflicts: The only first-hand Wuli-Wuli source, Holmer 1983 (sec. 2.9, p. 5, applied to Wuli-Wuli via sec. 10.3 p. 39), says stress is not significant and describes only a survey-wide 'tendency' to stress the second syllable in longer words; the catalog's rule string (second stress) codes this as fixed second-syllable. Watson 1944 (p. 8), for the neighbouring Kabi/Wakka/Yugarabul/Yugumbir vocabularies, gives accent generally on the first syllable with a weaker accent on the third, and Kite & Wurm 2004 (p. 22, Duungidjawu, a Waga-Waga dialect like Wuli-Wuli) give initial primary stress with secondary on odd syllables. So both non-Wuli-Wuli sources for the same dialect group place stress initially, against Holmer's second-syllable tendency, and Holmer himself says stress is not significant. Neither Watson nor Austlang says anything about Wuli-Wuli itself.

Wuli-Wuli phonology sec. 10.3 p. 39: phonetic system 'the same as that of Wakka-Wakka and Barunggam'; secs 10.3-10.8 and the whole Wakka-group part (pp. 22-96) contain no further stress/accent remark. sources.citation: Kite, Suzanne and Stephen Wurm. 2004. The Duungidjawu language of southeast Queensland: grammar, texts and vocabulary. Pacific Linguistics 553. Canberra: ANU. (sec. 1.2 + Table 1.1 pp. 3-4: Duungidjawu and Wuli-Wuli listed as mutually intelligible dialects of the 'Waga-Waga language'; sec. 2.3 'Stress' p. 22)
sources.note: For Duungidjawu (duun1241), not Wuli-Wuli: 'In polysyllabic words with no long vowels, primary stress falls on the first syllable, and secondary stress falls on odd numbered syllables (e.g. yanjarim 'old woman'). All long vowels bear stress.. If the long vowel is in the second syllable of a word, however, this syllable takes primary stress and the first syllable takes secondary stress (e.g. biya:yu 'two').' (p. 22). Also lists the only other Wuli-Wuli primary material: Hall n.d.b, AIATSIS pMS 6654 (c. 80 words + phrases from Queenie Meldrum, Hawkwood Station).
